activity.title: I wanted to take a moment to share the machine learning project I built as a part of the UC Berkeley School of Information MIDS DATASCI261 Machine Learning @ Scale course, "Predicting Flight Delays". Utilizing Databricks Serverless Compute provisioned by the course administrator, my team and I processed ~31 million flight records and ~600 million weather data points using Spark's machine learning packages to predict flight delays in real-time. Of the machine learning models we employed, our XGBoost model with walk-forward tuning over rolling yearly windows achieved the best MSE of 31.36 and an MAE of 12.02 minutes, meaning our predictions were only off by an average of ~12 minutes of the actual delayed minutes. This was a deeply complex business problem that mirrors the datasets and techniques used by real airline companies to model delays, which can cost hundreds of millions of dollars per year in logistical costs. Some highlighted skills my team and I learned were being able to implement time-series analysis in our feature engineering and processing data at scale using Spark and Databrick's distributed parallel compute. Thank you to my professor Vinicio De Sola and my team members Nadaa M. , Thomas Leffler , Ashwin Iyer , Ricky Pereira, and Jefferson J. for putting together an incredible project. You can view our final notebook at this repo: https://lnkd.in/gnxPktDP Download the HTML Final Report from the /reports folder: https://lnkd.in/gWrWF3xx

Imagine being surrounded by some of the most bright and brilliant Muslim women founders in San Francisco. Sharing ideas, struggles, and aspirations where you are met with full support and encouragement. What Nadaa M. and Almeena Shaikh, MS are building at Minaret is absolutely beautiful and filled my heart. Last night, I attended a lovely, intimate dinner where I met like-minded women who encouraged me to be my full self, not to pigeon-hole into this-or-that. You will never be called on to shrink yourself in the company of these women, and you will not be left alone to "build in a silo." You will meet women who want to lift you up, see you succeed, and do their best to connect you in all the ways that can make it happen. Thank you for such a beautiful evening ❤️ and thank you to Alif for the space.

Why you? Why this? Why now? Three questions. Most people can't answer all three without flinching. I almost talked myself out of going. But I showed up, answered all three, and placed second at pitch night with The Tech Bros . Here's what stuck with me more than the placement: I noticed a lot of women in that room struggling with just the first one. Not because we're not qualified. Because we've been trained to shrink. We second-guess our ideas. We call it imposter syndrome. We normalize it. And then we move on without fixing it. Meanwhile the guys are high-fiving each other across the room telling everyone their idea is genius. And honestly? That confidence works. We don't need to become them. But we do need to learn to show up for ourselves the way we show up for everyone else. And then start showing up for each other the same way. That's what spaces like The Tech Bros trying to build. Hard conversations. Real community. People rooting for each other. Thank you to the incredible panelists Roseanne Wincek Jing Kuang Nare Janvelyan, PhD Theresa (Wei) Dai Julia Lam AngelList and Irin Son for hosting! and a special thank you to Milette Gillow for bringing us all together.

💸 How I saved 95% of AI API costs for my first design partner! 💸 I used an underrated approach: systematic evaluations. When RAG was starting to gain traction in the industry, I realized that implementing it well was driving me crazy. There are so many parameters you have to choose, not just the prompt and the model but also things like the number of documents to retrieve, the retrieval method to use, and so on. I thought, couldn't I just find a tool that tries all the possibilities and tells me what works? No tool was doing that because it's impossible. You simply can't try everything. It would practically take an infinite amount of time. Okay, but probably not everything is worth trying, right? Then, I built a set of rules, grounded in research, that allowed me to avoid evaluating everything while still trying all the sound possibilities. This methodology helped my design partner to find a model 6x cheaper and a context optimisation strategy cutting token by 4x while still keeping the same accuracy.

Good HR work asks us to hold things that can feel in tension: consistency and individual circumstances, accountability and support, policy and humanity, urgency and thoughtfulness. That's what I keep coming back to a month into a new chapter as Assistant Superintendent of Human Resources at Travis Unified School District. Since July 1, I've mostly been listening, learning, and asking a lot of questions — working to understand the people and culture that make Travis such a special community. The move into HR feels both new and familiar. New because there is so much to learn. Familiar because the heart of the work has been at the center of my leadership for years: people, relationships, fairness, difficult conversations, and creating the conditions for others to do their best work. I'm grateful to be doing that alongside a talented team that cares deeply about getting it right. As we start a new school year, I'm focused on strengthening relationships across Travis and helping build an HR culture where people feel supported, expectations are clear, and decisions are grounded in both integrity and care.

YC rejected me 4 times. So on my fifth application, I Rick Rolled them. From 2016, I applied to Y Combinator every batch. Rejected every time. Most times we didn't even get a call. Then in December 2017, I woke up to a DM from Sam Altman: "We're interested in what you're doing." Paul Graham had told him Replit was important. After four rejections, they were recruiting us. Then Sam said: apply anyway. The batch starts tomorrow. Fill out that form. A fifth time. I was annoyed. So I did basic answers. And where it asked for a video, I pasted a YouTube link. Rick Astley. Never Gonna Give You Up. I walked into the interview the next day feeling like it was a formality. Michael Seibel shook my hand a little too hard. I sat down. First words out of his mouth: "Why did you Rick Roll us?" He was furious. The partners had been fuming while we waited outside. The next 10 minutes were brutal. Every question sharper than the last. And all I could think was: they have no idea who I am. They see an entitled tech guy, not an immigrant who spent years scraping his way here. I walked out and told my wife it was over. Called an Uber. Back to work. Before it arrived, my phone rang. "You got in. Come back - kickoff is about to start." Would not recommend this method for getting into YC though.

Dear Spindrift Beverage Co, Inc. , I am writing to you on behalf of our office fridge, and frankly, on behalf of many office fridges in America. Please replace the lemon flavor in the 4-flavor pack. It is consistently neglected, and the subsequent buildup of lemon cans in our office fridge is concerning. Unsettling, even. My team members and I have resorted to drinking one every few days, begrudgingly, as part of our civic duty to reduce lemon spindrift buildup. We are outnumbered by these cans and at risk of coup. Raspberry Lime and Mango Orange go quickly, and Grapefruit is next best. Lemon stays on the shelves, perpetually. Nobody reaches for it on purpose. Please add a replacement flavor (we suggest Fiji Apple or Pineapple). Or perhaps, your team can implement a Spindrift swap service, so we can give our cans away to other offices in exchange for better flavors. We believe there is a market here. The people have spoken. Thank you for your consideration. Evidence attached below.

Most obstetric clinics can tell you exactly how many births they did last year 🤰. Few can tell you how those women are doing nine months later ⁉️ . Fewer still can tell you the real number of birth injuries in that clinic ⁉️ 💸 . The thread between these events has never been built. And it's important for care management, for future pregnancies, for adherence to conservative treatment (which means saving 💸 and improving lives). The Australian Birth Trauma study showed just how expensive birth injury is to the woman, healthcare system, workplace and hospital (link in comments) A$17.5B 😵‍💫 Around 1 in 4 first-time mothers sustain anal sphincter damage during birth. 1 in 5 are missed even when a specialist examines her. They surface years later, in someone else's clinic, or in her next pregnancy with you. These injuries aren't invisible. Women feel them, the next birth is impacted by them. These injuries are instead missable, and whether one gets missed comes down to follow up care of women after birth, knowing her normal and asking the right questions. I've spent my career building AI that finds these injuries on ultrasound. It's shared commercially. And it's still not the solution to the problem. The answer is upstream. So that's what we're building with Pelby . Because her story is what protects her sister, her friend who isn't ready for children yet, her cousin, and even her daughter, one day. We're opening founding partner places for UK/US obstetric clinics. → The missing link between antenatal care, birth, and what happens next → Collection and analysis done for you, nothing extra for your team → See how your clinic compares on maternal outcomes and satisfaction → Early access to our risk models on approval If you deliver babies and you can't answer with confidence the question in line two, DM me. #PelvicHealth #Obstetrics #MaternalHealth #Urogynecology #WomensHealth #pelvicfloor #maternalsatisfication #obgyn #preventativehealth #predictivemodelling
